title: The smallest bone in your body is a 3 mm stirrup inside your ear
body: The stapes is the smallest and lightest bone in the human body, measuring roughly **2 to 3 mm**, and it is named after the stirrup it resembles. It is the last of the three middle-ear ossicles: the malleus (hammer) picks up vibrations from the eardrum and passes them to the incus (anvil), and the stapes pushes on the oval window that leads into the fluid-filled inner ear. Together the three bones act as a lever and concentrate the eardrum's vibrations onto a much smaller area, which lets sound pass efficiently into the cochlear fluid instead of bouncing off it. A tiny muscle, the stapedius, helps hold the stapes steady.

slides.heading: Match each ear bone to its nickname
slides.explanation: The three ossicles are named for their shapes. Sound travels from the eardrum to the malleus, on to the incus, then to the stapes and into the inner ear.

slides.heading: How a sound reaches your inner ear

steps.label: The stapes (stirrup) pushes the oval window

slides.heading: Why three tiny bones?
slides.text: Sound travelling from air into liquid mostly bounces off. The ossicles work as a lever, and they gather the force from the whole eardrum onto the much smaller oval window, so the vibrations become stronger but travel a shorter distance. This impedance matching lets sound energy pass into the cochlear fluid.

slides.heading: Which of these is not a middle-ear bone?
slides.explanation: The hyoid sits in the throat and anchors the tongue. The malleus, incus and stapes are the three ossicles of the middle ear, and the stapes is the smallest bone in the body.

slides.label: the length of the stapes
slides.text: It is the smallest and lightest bone in the body and transmits vibrations from the incus to the oval window. The stapedius muscle, supplied by the facial nerve, helps stabilise it.
